question: This workspace has a measured, embarrassing track record with its own controls: sixteen have been added, sixteen were wrong on their first version, thirteen failed OPEN — passing when they should have refused — and NOT ONE was ever found by the case it was built to catch. Every single one was found by running the case it was supposed to stay silent on. That lesson was written into the learning log three times and kept happening anyway, twice in one afternoon while fixing a criticism that the controls here only advise. So it became a gate: guard-coverage.mjs requires every script that can exit non-zero to have BOTH a refusal assertion and a silent assertion in the suite, and the main gate fails without them. On its first run it found four controls with no fixtures at all, including itself, and it was then wrong three times in the same family — it recognised only one spelling of an assertion, it required a minimum string length that missed assertions built from loop variables, and its own probe was named as a literal in the test file so it found 'assertions' for the probe and called it covered. Do not congratulate any of that. Answer four things, hard. (1) guard-coverage checks that both directions are ASSERTED. Name the classes of defect that survive it completely — a control can have a refusal fixture and a silent fixture and still be wrong how? Be specific and rank by how likely each is to be present here right now. (2) Thirteen of sixteen failed OPEN. Is that a coincidence of this codebase, or is there a structural reason controls written by a language model fail open — and if structural, what changes about how they should be written, not tested. (3) The workspace now has roughly eleven controls, sixteen skills, nine board stages, eight hooks and three suites. Is it past the point where adding another control makes it better, and what is the evidence either way? Take a position. (4) Given all of the above, name the single highest-value thing to do next to this workspace — and it may be 'remove something' or 'stop'.

reviews.lost: Response D’s useful later-stage refusal ledger, which could measure real operational value after the immediate wiring audit establishes that controls work at all.

reviews.minority: Response C's observation that the actual benefit of the existing control stack on unstaged, real developer code is completely unmeasured (0 recorded live catches), meaning the controls currently represent a pure token and maintenance tax.
reviews.lost: Response C's crucial insight on detection bias—that fail-open defects dominated the historical log primarily because the workspace's explicit testing discipline prioritized running silent cases.

reviews.minority: B's survivorship mechanism — fail-closed defects block real work, self-report, and get fixed off the books, so the *counted* defect population skews open even if write-time errors don't — a distinct, additive explanation of 13/16 no one else has.
reviews.lost: A leans on "zero live catches" as evidence the controls don't earn their keep; C's correction — that a control guarding a rare, severe boundary can correctly fire zero times, so absence of live refusals measures frequency, not protection — is lost, and with it the reason a refusal ledger is a bad deletion criterion.
